paras: The killing of Warren Bennett was the shooting of a Black youth of about sixteen while he hoed cotton at the Hickory Tavern Crossroads in Laurens County, South Carolina, on the morning of July 9, 1885. A coroner's jury returned a verdict against persons unknown, and a murder warrant later sworn out against a young white man, Wade Bolt, led to no reported arrest. The News and Courier made the case a centerpiece of its investigation of lawlessness in Laurens County, calling it one of the most atrocious crimes ever committed in the State.

According to the News and Courier's special correspondent, who relied on local men who asked not to be named, Bennett's stepfather, Steve Sullivan, had caught Bolt, then nineteen, with Bennett's crippled sister the previous spring, and Bennett had later scuffled with Bolt over it. In June, by the same account, three young white men tried to bribe Bennett to slander Bolt's sisters, and when he refused they spread the story as his own words; a boy who heard the offer later admitted this.

About 7 o'clock on the morning of July 9, Bennett was working in a field on J. E. Tumblin's place, about ten steps from a fence lined by a strip of woods. Mrs. Tumblin, working about seventy-five yards away, testified that she heard a shot and saw him fall, and that a man dressed in black with a slouch hat then ran from the fence and shot him again as he lay on the ground. She said she did not recognize the man but took him for white by the color of his hands, and a girl with her gave similar testimony. Dr. J. S. Wolf found that one ball had passed through both lungs and another had entered the back of the head, apparently from a .36 or .38 calibre pistol.

Informants told the correspondent that a neighbor, Mr. Clark, had seen Bolt, dressed in black, pass that morning asking for Epps Hellams and heard shots a few minutes later, and that Bolt then left with Hellams for a Sunday-school celebration.

Trial Justice Joel Ellison, acting as coroner, opened the inquest that evening, and on Saturday the jury found that Bennett died at the hands of persons unknown. Some told the correspondent that several jurors, and Ellison himself, were connected to the Bolt family, which others disputed and Ellison denied in a published letter. On the following Monday Sullivan swore out a warrant charging Bolt with the murder.

The correspondent wrote that the warrant was not sent out until Tuesday and that no hunt was made, while Ellison stated that the constable and then the sheriff searched without finding Bolt. No report of an arrest, indictment or trial of Bolt or Hellams appears in the coverage.

The first newspaper reports, as the correspondent summarized them, were brief and intimated that Bennett had been shot for speaking disrespectfully about some young ladies. The News and Courier then sent a correspondent whose long letter, headed 'Lack of Law in Laurens', set the killing beside the lynching of Charles Williams and other recent cases and called it 'The Dastardly Assassination of Warren Bennett'. He concluded that the evidence was 'certainly strong enough to secure his trial' and wrote that certain men in the county set little value on the lives of negroes. The Abbeville Press and Banner reprinted the letter and the News and Courier's editorial on August 5.

The editorial called the 'murder of the colored boy Warren Bennett' one of the most atrocious crimes in the State, blamed county officials who made no effort to arrest the suspects until they could escape, and warned that Black laborers were afraid to work in the fields alone. On August 28 the Springfield Weekly Republican in Massachusetts quoted Ellison's misspelled letter as 'a choice specimen' of South Carolina's trial justices and linked their poor quality to 'the epidemic of unpunished murders' in the state; no account of the killing from a Black newspaper appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Killing of Warren Bennett
bases: A Black youth was shot from ambush by a single gunman whom witnesses took for a white man, with a named white suspect; no mob, band or crowd is reported (A2, A3).

The News and Courier correspondent (A2) and Trial Justice Ellison's own published letter (A4) independently agree that Warren Bennett was killed and that a murder warrant was sworn out against Wade Bolt.

accounts.label: News and Courier special correspondent
accounts.gist: From interviews with unnamed local men and inquest witnesses, Bennett was ambushed after a quarrel with Wade Bolt over Bolt's relations with Bennett's crippled sister; circumstantial evidence pointed to Bolt, and officials let him get away.

accounts.label: Inquest testimony
accounts.gist: Mrs. Tumblin and a girl saw Bennett fall and an unrecognized man in black, taken for white, shoot him again; the jury returned a verdict against persons unknown.

accounts.label: Trial Justice Ellison's letter
accounts.gist: Ellison said he issued the warrant on Sullivan's oath, that the constable and then the sheriff searched for Bolt without success, and that he was not related to the Bolt family.

accounts.label: Early newspaper reports
accounts.gist: As summarized by the correspondent, first reports said Bennett was shot from behind a fence and intimated he had spoken disrespectfully about some young ladies.

framing.detail: The News and Courier headlined 'The Dastardly Assassination of Warren Bennett' and its correspondent judged the evidence 'strong enough to secure his trial' of Bolt.
The News and Courier editorial called it 'one of the most atrocious crimes ever committed in this State' and blamed county officials for letting suspects escape.
The Springfield Weekly Republican cited Ellison's letter as 'a choice specimen' of low-quality trial justices amid 'the epidemic of unpunished murders' in South Carolina.

versions.value: Warrant not dispatched until Tuesday and no hunt made for Bolt
Constable proceeded as soon as possible, several searches made, then sheriff searched, all without finding Bolt

conflicts.note: A4 is Ellison's own defense of his conduct; A2 is the correspondent's account from local informants.

conflicts.field: Ellison's relation to the Bolt family

versions.value: Correspondent was told Ellison was related or closely connected to Bolt's family, which others questioned

conflicts.note: A2 reports hearsay in both directions; A4 is Ellison's denial.

versions.value: Eight jurors were relatives or connections of Bolt
Four jurors (Armstrong, Pleas Bolt, Stobo Bolt, Knight) were, per a man who challenged the claim

conflicts.note: Both versions are hearsay reported by the correspondent.

versions.value: Bennett had spoken disrespectfully about some young ladies (first newspaper reports)
The story was invented by three young white men after Bennett refused their bribe; he was guiltless

conflicts.note: The correspondent credits the second version, said to be admitted by a boy who heard the bribe offer.

record_check.dossier: Ambush killing by a single gunman (suspected white individual); no mob reported
Inquest verdict was 'persons unknown', but a murder warrant named Wade Bolt, a white man of nineteen, and Epps Hellams was also suspected
Individual(s): one gunman seen, taken for a white man
Rumor that he spoke disrespectfully about young ladies, reported as fabricated
Three items in the Abbeville Press and Banner (reprinting the News and Courier) and one in the Springfield Weekly Republican

info: Thursday, 9 July 1885, about 7 o'clock in the morning
In a cotton field on J. E. Tumblin's place at the Hickory Tavern Crossroads, about ten steps from a fence bordered by a strip of woods
Warren Bennett, 'a negro youth of about sixteen years of age', a farm worker on Tumblin's place

Early newspaper reports intimated he had spoken disrespectfully about some young ladies; the correspondent's informants said three young white men had invented the report after Bennett refused their bribe to say it, and called him guiltless
One man dressed in black with a slouch hat, taken for white by the color of his hands; local belief named Wade Bolt, a white man of nineteen, with some crediting Epps Hellams with managing it
